paragraphs: The Australian Museum (AMS) Ichthyology Collection might well be the largest in the Southern Hemisphere. Located in Sydney, Australia, it is split between two storage sites: one in the Sydney CBD and the other at the Castle Hill Discovery Centre.

The collection houses fish from both larval and adult stages of life. Larvae counts push past a million, while adult specimens number closer to 750,000. The AMS Ichthyology Collections boast  2,500 Type specimens - dating back to the 1800s. It has the 4th largest collection of Primary Type specimens in the world! Historically, many species were described based off of efforts made by researchers at the AMS fish collection.

The geographic scope of the AMS fish collections focuses on the Indio-Pacific region, with particular strengths in New South Wales, the Great Barrier Reef, temperate rocky reefs, mesopelagic waters from the upper slope to 1000m depth, and Indo-Pacific Islands. However, they possess taxa from all continents and oceans.

Gilbert Percy Whitley (1903-1975) was a prolific author and AMS collection builder. From 1925 to his retirement in 1964, Whitley registered some 37,000 specimens, at an annual average of almost 950 specimens, virtually doubling the size of the collection. Considering he personally identified, registered, and tagged all the specimens and concurrently wrote 500+ papers, and described 451 species of fishes, the effort is indeed impressive.

Most lots are housed long-term in 70% ethanol, though the museum also collects dried material, photographs, and radiographs. In recent years, AMS has built up genetic stores of frozen and alcohol-fixed tissues.

The Australian Museum Ichthyology Collection is 100% computerized and can be found within the Atlas of Living Australia ( https://www.ala.org.au/ ).  Some AMS fish collection data can be found on FishNet 2 using institution code AM (though the code has officially been updated to AMS). We look forward to continuing our partnership with this incredible trove of fish biodiversity!
Image: Stuart Humphreys @ Australian Museum
Image: Abram Powell @ Australian Museum
Image: Abram Powell @ Australian Museum
Image: Abram Powell @ Australian Museum
Image: James King @ Australian Museum
Established in 2019, the Berkley Museum of Vertebrate Zoology (MVZ) Fishes Collection is the youngest ichthyology collection in the United States!

Inside the Berkley MVZ, there are more than 14,500 individual specimens contained in over 780 lots. Utilizing fluid-preservation methods, museum personnel take care to ensure DNA will remain extractable from most specimens in the future. A handful of fish have also been photographed or micro-CT scanned, and MVZ keeps a small of dried material.

Curator of Fishes, Dr. Chris Martin, studies the ecology, evolution, and genomics of adaptive radiation in fishes. His primary research sites, in the Caribbean and West Africa, serve as the origins of many specimens found in the MVZ collection.

Common uses of the collection include genomic sequencing, functional morphology, morphometrics, systematics, course-based undergraduate research experiences, and ecological studies using stomach contents and stable isotope analysis.
The MVZ Fishes collection is digitized, data records can be found on their Arctos at https://arctos.database.museum/search.cfm?guid_prefix=MVZ%3AFish

Great news - the Berkley Museum of Vertebrate Zoology is one of FishNet 2’s newest data partners! We are overjoyed to have them in our network and already have a subset of their data available through our site, www.fishnet2.net, using institution code MVZ.

The Canadian Museum of Nature Fish Collection, founded in 1958 by Dr. Donald McAlister in Ottawa, Canada, houses approximately 760,000 fish specimens. This extensive collection includes fluid-preserved lots, a large otolith assemblage, dried preparations, radiograph images, and photos. Notably, the museum is home to the National Cryobank of Canada and contains a significant amount of fish tissues. Recognized as a Center of Excellence for its Arctic collections, the museum published the field guide "Marine Fishes of Arctic Canada" in 2018, based on specimens from its own collection. In addition, it holds the world's best collection of lampreys and an impressive assortment of deep-water eelpouts.

While primarily utilized for research, the Canadian Museum of Nature Fish Collection actively engages in educational and outreach initiatives. Public display areas allow visitors to marvel at select specimens based on current themes. Furthermore, the museum hosts an annual open house, connecting with the local community and showcasing ongoing work. The collection spearheads multiple interdisciplinary research projects, including collaborative efforts with the Invertebrate department. These projects delve into the study of glochidia and sturgeon fishes in Ontario, serving as population surveys and adding to the collection. Another collaboration focuses on identifying Arctic fishes collected by the Federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans, contributing vital information about the ecology of fishes in this unique region.
The Canadian Museum of Nature Fish Collection publishes data to GBIF, and can be found at:  ipt.nature.ca
We are proud to be partnering with The Canadian Museum and will eventually display this data on FishNet 2 as well.
Find out more at: https://nature.ca/en/our-science/collections/zoology-collections/

The Florida Biodiversity Collection (FBC) Ichthyology Collection is a branch of the (FWC) Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. This state collection is representative of Florida's fish biodiversity spanning from 1955 to the present day, though the oldest specimens within the FBC collection date back to 1950. Presently, the Florida Biodiversity Collection’s Ichthyology Collection houses an impressive array of over 37,000 lots, containing about 120,000 individual fish. Approximately 80% of the collection comprises fish from marine and estuarine habitats, while the remaining 20% are found in freshwater environments. The specimens encompass all life stages, from larval to juvenile, to adulthood.

This collection roots back to the endeavors of biologists Victor Springer and Kenneth Woodburn. Their survey of the biodiversity of fish and invertebrates in Tampa Bay in 1955 laid the foundation for the FBC. Almost 5,000 lots were collected during the years 1965 to 1967, via the Hourglass expeditions that ventured into the Gulf, offshore of Tampa Bay.

Steady growth persisted through the '70s, and in 1982, the Southeast Area Monitoring and Assessment Program (SEAMAP) began. This program, a collaborative effort funded at the federal level in partnership with the FWRI, strides towards the shared goal of acquiring and utilizing scientific insights concerning marine resources. Over the next three decades, SEAMAP embarked on multiple collections each year. The SEAMAP Ichthyoplankton Collection falls under the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) jurisdiction but is managed and administered by the FBC. The SEAMAP Ichthyoplankton collection amount to over 580,000 cataloged lots. Discover more about SEAMAP at: https://myfwc.com/.../specimen-collections/fishes/seamap/

Interns from the University of South Florida can be found helping out around the FBC collection. In the upcoming years, FBC Ichthyology Collection staff hope to form new collaborations and expand their sampling efforts to encompass more inland fishes of the Florida freshwater rivers and springs, as well as to the deep sea.

The data housed within the Florida Biodiversity Collection’s Ichthyology Collection are available through their internal database (https://webportal.specifycloud.org/fwrf/) and a portion are accessible through FishNet 2, using the institution code FSBC.
Find out more about this outstanding ichthyology collection on their site, https://myfwc.com/.../specimen.../fishes/ichthyology/

Located in Suitland, Maryland, the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History (NMNH) Fish Collection stands as one of the most esteemed repositories of fish biodiversity. Housing approximately 6 million specimens, it boasts the world's largest collections of North American, Neotropical, Caribbean, and West Pacific fish fauna - with notable strengths in the Coral Triangle and French Polynesia, as well as a long research history of Latin American neotropical fishes.

While the majority of fish specimens are stored in ethanol, the collection also encompasses osteological, cleared and stained, and DNA preparations. Complementing these specimen lots, the NMNH Fish Collection houses an extensive archive of color photographs, x-ray images, illustrations, and invaluable field notes.

Among their collections, the NMNH Fish Collection proudly cares for a coelacanth specimen, a fish steeped in evolutionary significance. Yet, when pressed to identify the collection's true pride, curators point to its comprehensive representation of 75% of all known fish species.  The NMNH partners with the National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

Looking towards the future, the NMNH Fish Collection is eager to nurture the next generation of Smithsonian ichthyologists. There is currently an open call (through September 2023) for Post-Doctoral Fellows interested in Systematic Ichthyology.
The Smithsonian Institute NMNH Fish Collection is a FishNet 2 Partner and periodically provides data to our repository.
They also publish data through their own database (https://collections.nmnh.si.edu/search/fishes/)
and GBIF (https://www.gbif.org/.../fc904fab-a33c-4ca8-bd23...)
Find out more about this incredible fish collection at: https://naturalhistory.si.edu/.../vertebrate-zoology/fishes
The Arkansas State University Museum of Zoology (ASUMZ) Ichthyology Collection is located in Jonesboro, Arkansas, within the Arkansas Center for Biodiversity Collections (ACBC).

85-95% of this collection are Arkansas fishes, it is particularly rich in species from the Ozark Mountain region. ASUMZ‘s individual specimens number over 213,000. This collection is one of the largest of fish in Arkansas. Most of ASUMZ's growth took place from 1965-1999, under professors Dr. John K. Beetles and Dr. George L. Harp. Their work was instrumental in the creation of the state study Fishes of Arkansas (Robison and Buchanan 1988; 2nd edition 2020), a staple text in Arkansas and the surrounding states for identifying fishes and teaching ichthyology. Today, Dr. Brook Fluker,

In 2016, the National Science Foundation granted ASUMZ Ichthyology Collection support for specimens' restoration, databasing, and georeferencing. Today, the majority of ASUMZ’s ichthyology collection data are georeferenced and imaged, in part via collaboration with TUBRI’s biodiversity informatics branch. The ASUMZ Collection is online via Arctos, and we look forward to hosting this data on FishNet 2 in the near future.
Find out more at: https://www.astate.edu/college/sciences-and-mathematics/departments/biology/Arkansas-Center-for-Biodiversity-Collections/

The North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences (official abbreviation: NCSM) houses an outstanding ichthyology collection, with the oldest fish specimen dating back to 1850. Established in the 1940s, this collection has become a pivotal repository for understanding the historical fish biodiversity in North Carolina and beyond.

Comprising over 1.4 million specimens, the NCSM ichthyology collection is one of the largest and most diverse in the southeastern United States. With a regional focus on SE US fishes, this collection houses comprehensive records of fish biodiversity from the Blue Ridge Mountains to the Atlantic Ocean - along with a diverse sampling of specimens from 65 other countries. In recent years, the collection has grown with the acquisition of various orphaned collections which have greatly increased the marine holdings, notably from the deep-sea. Most lots within the NCSM ichthyology collection are fluid-preserved, though they also collect skeletal materials.

As scientific advancements continue, the museum ensures its relevance by embracing modern research techniques and emerging fields of study - steadily growing its store of ethanol-preserved tissues for DNA studies. Ensuring the accessibility of their resources to the global scientific community, museum personnel have meticulously computerized their specimens and published data to their internal database, as well as multiple aggregates such as GBIF, VertNet, and FishNet 2.
Learn more about this outstanding fish collection on the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences website: https://naturalsciences.org/.../ichthyology-collection
Explore their internal database:
https://collections.naturalsciences.org/search/ichthyology
Connect with them on  Instagram, and Twitter @NaturalSciences

Located in Makhanda in South Africa’s Eastern Cape Province, the South African Institute for Aquatic Biodiversity (SAIAB) is an internationally renowned institution dedicated to the study of aquatic biodiversity. SAIAB is one of 5 national facilities of the National Research Foundation (NRF).

SAIAB is the custodian of the National Fish Collection of South Africa. This collection ranks among the largest in the southern hemisphere and is the largest repository of southern African fishes globally. This impressive collection boasts 122,466 lots, containing approximately 1,021,475 individual fish specimens. The collection is cared for within the JLB Smith Collection Management Centre, a facility named in honor of the renowned ichthyologist who first identified the living coelacanth. In 2007 a new Collection Facility was constructed, marking the beginning of a new era in the long history of ichthyology in South Africa.
Researchers who work with these specimens attest to the care and preservation standards upheld by SAIAB. Specimens dating back as far as the late 19th century are still in remarkable condition.

Among extensive chondrichthyan collections, there is a wholly preserved albino great white shark! The National Fish Collection is also widely known for its assemblage of historical coelacanth specimens. The second coelacanth ever collected is proudly on display in one of the front rooms of the facility.
As part of the collection process, samples are taken from collected fish specimens to extract DNA for SAIAB’s Biobank. The DNA information can then be linked to corresponding collection lots.
SAIAB receives both Biobank and National Fish Collection loan requests from scientists around the world!
SAIAB is committed to the open sharing and dissemination of its data, which are made available through the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF).
You can access their data at [https://www.gbif.org/grscicoll/institution/a90ba963-9569-4b96-8d56-452aa7b83f75]
We are delighted to announce our partnership with this esteemed aquatic biodiversity research institute and will be providing access to their valuable data in the upcoming version of our website.
For further information, please visit [https://saiab.ac.za/]
or explore their engaging YouTube channel at [www.youtube.com/@southafricaninstituteforaq7307]

The Louisiana State University Museum of Natural Science (LSUMNS) Ichthyology Collection has housed preserved fish specimens since 1979. Recent NSF-funded renovations to Foster Hall, on the LSU campus in Baton Rouge, have brought the collection under the same roof as LSU’s other vertebrate specimen and tissue collections and improved accessibility to LSU students and visiting researchers. Today, the ichthyology collection is a repository for specimens from all major groups of living fishes in the world.

LSUMNS’s steadily growing collection numbers approximately 390,000 fish specimens within 22,000 lots. Significant collection efforts have taken place in the northern Gulf of Mexico, though the collection’s scope extends across the globe from the Hawaiian Islands and Central and South America to Southeast Asia, Australia and the Indo-West Pacific. LSUMNS also has strong holdings of fishes from Louisiana’s fresh waters, although these are dwarfed by those of nearby Tulane University’s Royal D. Suttkus Ichthyology Collection.

Most lots are preserved in 70% ethanol, though LSUMNS keeps ichthyological collections of fossils, dried specimens, cleared and stained specimens, photographs, radiographs, and field notes.  Ichthyology collection curator, Dr. Prosanta Chakrabarty, studies the evolutionary history of fishes by studying their morphology and through use of genomics, among other tools. His lab travels internationally multiple times a year—its work resulting in LSUMNS having one of the largest and most diverse collections of fish tissue and DNA in the United States; containing over 10,000 samples from more than 1,500 species. These genetic resources are accessible online at:  www.lsu.edu/mns/collections/genetic-resources.php
Find out more about this impressive ichthyology collection on their website:
www.lsu.edu/mns/collections/ichthyology.php
For more information about Dr. Chakrabarty’s lab, please see: www.prosanta.org/

As a long-standing partner of FishNet 2, you can explore LSUMNS’s fish records on our site using institution code LSUMZ. LSUMNS also shares data with VertNet and GBIF, further broadening their avenues of digital accessibility.

The Division of Fishes at the Field Museum of Natural History (acronym: FMNH) in Chicago, Illinois, has a rich history and an extensive collection. Established in 1894, this impressive assortment is comprised of over 1,750,000 individual specimens; 130,000 lots; 10,000 species; 4,500 tissue samples; 5,600 paratype lots; 3,500 skeletons; 890 primary type lots; and 450 families. Additionally, it holds physical collections of radiographs, photographs, and field notes. Efforts to digitize photo collections are underway.

With a long history of dedicated curators, the Division of Fishes at FMNH houses fish from all over the globe -  you will find a wide range of freshwater fishes, from catfishes to cichlids, as well as diverse assemblages of reef fishes. It would be remiss not to mention the lobe-finned gems cared for by the Field Museum: the legendary coelacanth and, common ancestor of all tetrapods, the lungfish.

Caleb McMahan, the current curator, is as dedicated to this collection as his predecessors; his work has helped it grow via collaborative international fieldwork in the freshwaters of the Neotropics, primarily in Central America and Mexico. Newly collected specimens and those from the historical collection are utilized to investigate topics such as systematics, taxonomy, historical biogeography, and body shape evolution.
At present, the Field Museum of Natural History hosts its ichthyology collection data on GBIF: https://www.gbif.org/dataset/afc30a94-6107-488a-b9c0-ba9c4fa68b7c
Excitingly - the Field Museum is eager to become a new partner of FishNet 2, and we are eager to have them! FMNH data will eventually be hosted on our site, under code FMNH.
Find out more at: https://www.fieldmuseum.org/science/research/area/fishes/fishes-history
Tulane University's Royal D. Suttkus Fish Collection is, numerically, the world's largest collection of (post-larval) fishes!

The origin of the modern fish collection can be traced back to 1950 when ichthyologist (and eponym of the collection), Royal D. Suttkus, joined Tulane’s faculty and began building up from just 2 dried specimens remaining from Tulane’s earliest natural history collections (originating in the 1880s).

Though specimens hail from most fish major groups and continents in the world, Suttkus sampled the US Gulf Coast River drainages year after year for 50 years, particularly in the states of Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Florida, Arkansas, Tennessee, and Georgia. This area is very rich in freshwater fish diversity, and due to his efforts, Suttkus described 20 new fish species.

His collection method included keeping all that was found, leading to the staggering 8 million fish specimens housed today. Due to repeated sampling in the same localities and the catch-and-keep methodology, this collection is self-described as "specimen-rich, species-poor." For example, it contains approximately 1 million specimens of the same common minnow species, the black-tail shiner (Cyprinella venusta). Other common minnow species of these regions, such as the bullhead minnow, number in the hundreds of thousands. Fortunately, due to the high fecundity of these common species, their populations in situ have not been affected by Suttkus's collection methods; they remain the most common fish in these waterways. The specimen-rich status of this collection allows for a very complete picture of freshwater fish biodiversity in the Gulf Coast River drainages dating back many decades.

Digitization and georeferencing of the Royal D. Suttkus Fish Collection took place in the early 2000s under the direction of curator Dr. Henry Bart and informatics specialist Nelson Rios. These data are primarily hosted under FishNet 2 using institution code TU. To this day, the Royal D. Suttkus fish collection inspires biodiversity informatics projects by Tulane University Biodiversity Research Institute's biodiversity informatics team, headed by Dr. Yasin Bakis.
Find out more at http://www.tubri.org/fishes/

Located in Fayetteville, Arkansas, the University of Arkansas (UA) Museum’s Ichthyology collection dates back to 1968, with older specimens from the mid-1950s. UA’s fish collection is primarily fluid-preserved, with almost 6,000 specimens within 2,000 lots.  UA also houses fossil records and dried fish specimens. Primarily utilized for teaching ichthyology, the occasional lot emerges from storage to be placed on exhibition or to be sent off for an inquiry.

The species assemblages housed in the University Museum’s collection emphasize local Arkansas river fish. While a significant portion of their fishes were initially collected through campus research endeavors, the collaboration between the University and the U.S. Geological Service Arkansas Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit has resulted in an acquisition of fish from new areas in the state, such as the Buffalo River region.
UA Zoology collections are available online at https://uamuseum.omeka.net/
For more information visit https://fulbright.uark.edu/university-museum/collections.php

The first fishes were brought to the University of Kansas Biodiversity Institute (KUBI) in 1898, beginning what grew to become the KUBI Ichthyology voucher collection, official abbreviation KUI. KUBI also has a taxonomically and geographically diverse tissue collection with the acronym KUIT.  Today, hundreds of thousands of fish are housed in the state-of-the-art collection facilities of Dyche Hall - where the KUI Division benefits from access to shared morphological, molecular, imaging, and data analysis research facilities. The collection is managed by Andrew Bentley.

The University of Kansas is significant to FishNet 2 because FishNet originated at KU in 1999. The KU Division of Ichthyology started FishNet out of efforts to create a distributed information resource of North American flora and fauna. They ran it for 10 years until FishNet transitioned to a cache-based query infrastructure with its move to Tulane University in 2009 (when FishNet became FishNet 2). KU has remained a cherished FishNet 2 partner and will continue to play a role in guiding the future of our network as we head into a new era.
The collections are cataloged using Specify Software and are published to all major aggregators – GBIF, iDigBio, FishNet 2, VertNet, OBIS, and GGBN.

Approximately 680,000 voucher specimens and 11,000 tissue samples make up the KUBI Ichthyology Collection: with an emphasis on freshwater fishes from the Central United States. The collection houses over 2,600 freshwater, marine and estuarine species from over 80 countries and oceans with over 200 type specimens.  The collection is over 95% georeferenced.  The voucher collection comprises 526,000 wet preparations of 70% ethanol, with 8,000 cleared/stained, and over 2,000 skeletal specimens. Tissues are stored in cryogenic Dewars maintained as part of the Genetic Resources Facility.

A thorough record of ichthyological biodiversity from the Great Plains region has earned the KU Ichthyology Division recognition as a Regional Center in the Midwest and Great Plains region. Ongoing research is actively contributing to the continual growth of the collection’s size and scope. Current research endeavors within the KU Division of Ichthyology span niche-modeling studies, transcriptome-based studies of scorpionfishes, and the development of the caudal-fin to higher-level studies of ray-finned fishes, incorporating both fossil and extant species. Research is conducted under the supervision of Ichthyology Curator, William Leo Smith. Previous curators include Ed Wiley and Frank Cross.
You can find out more about this collection and perform web searches of KU fish vouchers or tissues on their website: https://biodiversity.ku.edu/ichthyology/collections
KU Ichthyology Collection data can also be browsed on FishNet 2 using institution code KU, or collection codes KUI and KUIT.

The University of North Alabama Fish Collection (UNAF) was originally established during the 1960s when a team of freshwater biologists set out to collect mussels and caught a few ancillary fish. The collection grew circuitously for a decade, then sat - mostly forgotten, except for use in teaching - for more than 30 years. Ichthyology professor Jeffery M. Ray came onto the scene in 2008 and began to build up the collection with surveys of local streams. UNAF, comprised of 4,000 specimens, is rich in freshwater species from Alabama, Mississippi, and Tennessee. In its fledgling state of digitization, the UNAF collection is working on inputting collection information into spreadsheets.  Dr. Ray has used FishNet 2 as a research tool for years, and we are proud to welcome the University of North Alabama Fish Collection as a new partner.

Located in Seattle, Washington, the University of Washington Fish Collection (UWFC) is housed within the UW School of Aquatic and Fisheries Sciences. Established in 1919, the collection contains 13,000,000 ichthyological specimens from all life stages: eggs, larvae, juvenile, and adults! The earlier lots in the collection date back to the 1880’s. Specimen preparations are mostly ethanol, though UWFC also houses tissue samples, skeletal material, scales, otoliths, cleared and stained lots, as well as locality data, radiographs, and photographs.

UWFC has impressive assemblages of regional fishes from the freshwaters of the Pacific Northwest, the Eastern North Pacific, and the Western Tropical Pacific. Over the years, they have expanded their scope by absorbing donated collections, and are currently incorporating Dr. Frank Pezold’s collection of global tropical fishes.
Utilizing and adding to this collection, current research is being done on the evolution of bony fishes by museum curator Dr. Luke Tornabene.

A pioneer in biodiversity informatics, the UWFC has had a searchable digital database since 1995! This collection is an established partner of FishNet2 and provides data to multiple aggregates such as VertNet and GBIF.
For more information visit: https://www.burkemuseum.org/collections-and-research/biology/ichthyology

The Cambridge Museum of Zoology (UMZC) traces its origins back to the year 1865, when the Museum of Comparative Anatomy merged with the collections of the Cambridge Philosophical Society. Many of the museum’s specimens were acquired between 1865 and 1915 when early expeditions brought back collections of fish and amphibians from Africa. However,  new material is added annually, particularly in recent years due to international collaborations.

Today, the UMZC ichthyology collection comprises approximately 7,000 lots of fish, mostly stored in spirit. Alongside UMZC’s wet collection are fossil and dried fishes, as well as histology slide preparations and models.

Remarkably, Darwin’s fish from the Beagle Voyage, described by 19th-century Cambridgeshire naturalist Leonard Jenyns, are housed in the UMZC ichthyology collection. Even today, these remain important for the taxonomy of South American species. Many of the forty specimens are types.

Other significant assemblages from within the UMZC are Chinese fish from the Vachell Collection, and African fish collected by J.S. Budgett, including historically important specimens that were used to document the development of the lungfish. Cambridge researchers are currently utilizing these specimens to study the mechanics of lungfish skulls, exploring the transition of vertebrates from sea to land.
FishNet 2 is honored to be partnering with this historical and esteemed collection.

Their data will be available on FN2 when our updated database is up and running. In the meantime, explore the Cambridge Museum of Zoology's internal database at:  https://www.museum.zoo.cam.ac.uk/collection/online
Find out more about this extraordinary collection at: https://www.museum.zoo.cam.ac.uk/recent-vertebrates

Founded in 1981, the Instituto de Pesquisas Científicas e Tecnológicas do Amapá (IEPA) Ichthyological Collection, maintains 5131 cataloged lots that offer rich insight into Amapá's diverse aquatic ecosystems. The Brazilian State of Amapá has incredibly rich aquatic biodiversity - within its three main river basins, fish from independent ecoregions cooccur. However much remains unstudied, in part because sampling sites can be difficult to access, requiring travel by boat into protected areas.

The IEPA collection encompasses specimens from all of Amapá’s municipalities, continental and coastal waters, and even extends to the neighboring state of Pará. Housed here are representatives from 21 orders, 66 families, and 293 genera, comprising 676 different species, including both confirmed nominal species and morphospecies awaiting expert confirmation.

Characiformes are the most abundant fish order, followed by Siluriformes, Cichliformes, and Gymnotiformes. IEPA maintains Holotypes and Paratypes of species pivotal to understanding Amapá's unique biodiversity, including those newly described. Collection curator Dr. Cecile Gama recently described a piranha with spots, named after a jaguar by popular local vote!

While traditionally fixed in formalin and preserved in alcohol, tissue batches for molecular studies preserved in alcohol and frozen are opening new avenues for research. The collection is computerized and has several lots made available through documented loans to specialist researchers from different groups who carry out their research activities in Brazil and other parts of the world.

The collection continues to grow, with over 2000 lots awaiting listing. FishNet 2 is incredibly proud and excited to partner with the IEPA collection, which offers a unique insight into Amazonian aquatic biodiversity. We cannot wait to help share their data with the world on the new version of our site -  coming soon.

Species with Holotypes (H) or Paratypes (P) deposited in the IEPA Ichthyological Collection. a) Laetacara flamannellus (P), b) Ammoglanis amapaensis (P/H), c) Phenacogaster apletostigma (P), d) Poecilia waiapi (P)
Storage location for lots from the IEPA Ichthyological Collection

The Amazon is the target of many studies regarding the taxonomy, systematics, ecology and distribution of fish and Amapá, despite its great diversity of fish, still has very little studied fish fauna.

The IEPA Ichthyological Collection began in 1981 with the first collections of specimens for scientific purposes and currently, its entire collection is digitized and packaged appropriately for taxonomic and systematic studies, consultations by specialists and loans. There are 5131 lots representing all municipalities in Amapá, continental and coastal waters and those close to the state of Pará. The collection houses specimens from 21 Orders, 66 Families, 293 Genera and 676 different species, including confirmed nominal species and morphospecies that require confirmation by experts.
The most abundant fish orders are the Characiformes, with 42.3% of all species present in the collection, followed by Siluriformes with 27.5%, Cichliformes with 11.4% and Gymnotiformes with 4.9%.
The IEPA Fish Collection also has Holotypes and Paratypes of species deposited in the collection relating to new species described for Amapá.

An increase in the maintenance of the IEPA Ichthyological Collection is expected so that its scientific role lasts over the years and is used by various sectors linked to science to uncover our still largely unknown biodiversity.

Amapá has a great diversity of fish, but its fauna is still little studied. In its three main river basins, fish species are found both considered Amazonian and belonging to the Guiana Shield and also inhabitants of the main channel of the Amazon River, considered independent ecoregions.

In 2005, with the accreditation of the Amapá Fauna Scientific Collection as a faithful depository of samples of components of the genetic heritage with the Genetic Heritage Management Council of the Ministry of the Environment (CGEN), the fish collection began to carry collection status official scientific research of the State of Amapá for the purpose of deposit by undertakings that may alter the aquatic environment, as an environmental condition and also to prove the existence of testimonial material for scientific publications, being able to carry out official shipments and remittances of copies to Brazil and the exterior.

The collection of the CCFA Ichthyological Collection is fully qualified, digitized in a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet with all the information relating to each batch, such as species, geographic coordinates, collector and date of collection, detailed location, determinant, project of origin, as well as other important information. This data was accessed to profile the collection.

The IEPA Fish Collection had its first specimen listed in 1981, deposited in the Ângelo Moreira Natural History Museum of “Costa Lima”. With the creation of IEPA – Institute of Studies and Research of Amapá-IEPA, which was later transformed into the Institute of Scientific and Technological Research of the State of Amapá, maintaining the acronym IEPA in 1988, it incorporated the Costa Lima Museum and all its collections, called Coleções Científicas Fauna do Amapá, a name that remains to this day.

At the end of the 1980s, the Ichthyological Collection's collection included approximately 1,100 batches of fish coming mainly from the Amapá Lakes Region and the Macacoari River, but also received specimens from the municipalities of Macapá and Santana.

The effort to capture fish increased considerably from the year 2000 onwards (Figure 1), when several taxonomic and ecological projects began that increased not only the number of specimens deposited, but also the diversity of species with greater representation of the territory of the region. state of Amapá.

The IEPA Ichthyological Collection houses collections from all municipalities in Amapá (Figure 2), with representatives from continental and coastal areas and those close to the State of Pará, in addition to freshwater and saltwater species. The municipalities that received the greatest sampling effort were Laranjal do Jari, Pracuúba and Macapá.

The specimens are captured using different techniques according to the characteristics of the sampled environment and are fixed in formalin and preserved in alcohol at 70°Gl, but currently, due to the difficulty in acquiring Formaldehyde and to guarantee the possibility of molecular studies, some specimens are also fixed in alcohol.

Our collection currently has 5131 deposited lots, containing specimens of fish belonging to all basins and main rivers in the state of Amapá, including specimens collected in the coastal region of the state and in several State and Federal Conservation Units. The batches are packaged in glass jars with screw caps according to their size and arranged on steel shelves (Figure 3) according to their systematic classification according to Fricke et al. (2021) in their own and constantly refrigerated environment. Very large specimens are numbered and placed in larger volume containers (Figure 4), properly sealed.

The IEPA Fish Collection houses specimens from 21 Orders, 66 Families, 293 Genera and 676 different species, including confirmed nominal species and morphospecies that require confirmation by specialists. Recently, the deposit of batches of tissue for molecular studies began, fixed and preserved in 96% alcohol and kept frozen. In addition to the lots listed in the collection, there are more than 2000 lots in the IEPA Ichthyology Laboratory from various projects already developed by IEPA awaiting listing.

The IEPA Fish Collection also has Holotypes and Paratypes of the species Laetacara flamannellus Ottoni, Bragança, Amorim and Gama 2012, Phenacogaster apletostigma Lucena and Gama 2007, Ammoglanis amapaensis Mattos, Costa and Gama 2008 and Poecilia waiapi Bragança, Costa and Gama 2012 ( Figure 6) deposited in the collection referring to new species described for Amapá. It has several lots made available through documented loans to specialist researchers from different groups who carry out their research activities in Brazil and other parts of the world.
These collections are used by researchers interested in studying anatomy, taxonomy, phylogenetic relationships, biogeography, macroecology and any other research involving fauna specimens.
